name: Neonatal jaundice
oneLine: The commonest colour of the first week, and telling the expected yellow from the dangerous one

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.blurb: Why the newborn turns yellow, and why the brain is at stake

chapters.title: Approach to the newborn and mother
chapters.blurb: Warm hands, warm room, and the mother as historian

chapters.title: Patient particulars
chapters.blurb: Hours of age, gestation and weight set the risk before a question is asked

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Record age in hours as well as days, gestation in completed weeks, and birth and current weight. A 30-hour-old preterm baby and a 5-day-old term baby with the same yellow carry entirely different risks, and weight loss since birth tells you about intake before feeding is even discussed.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: The clock, the spread, the feeds and the nappies

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Let the mother use her own words for the yellow: when she first saw it, where on the body, and whether it is deepening. Her clock time of onset is the single most valuable fact in the whole case.

skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.expect: Fix each complaint against hours of age: yellow since which hour, feeds how many times since morning, wet nappies counted, not estimated. Precision here replaces a battery of tests later.

chapters.title: Birth, feed, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Blood groups, the previous child, and the delivery behind the yellow

skill.hx.paed.neo.maternal_perinatal.expect: Ask blood groups of mother and baby with any antibody result, maternal diabetes or thyroid illness, and drugs around delivery. A group O mother with a group A or B baby reframes the whole case toward haemolysis.

skill.hx.paed.birth_natal_neonatal.expect: Ask gestation, birth weight, place of delivery, first cry and resuscitation, and any forceps or vacuum help with scalp swelling. An instrumental delivery explains yellow that appears after discharge home.

skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.expect: Ask about siblings who needed light treatment or blood exchange, and about favism, drug-triggered anaemia or lifelong mild jaundice in the family. A previously affected sibling is the strongest warning this baby will follow the same course.

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: Vigour, weight and the colour itself

skill.gen.paed.appearance.expect: Judge vigour first: a pink, active baby that cries lustily and roots for the breast argues against advanced disease, while a sleepy, floppy baby that must be woken for feeds is already showing brain effects of bilirubin.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.expect: Record temperature, heart rate, breathing rate and oxygen saturation with the weight of the day. Fever or fast breathing beside the yellow points to infection driving the jaundice, not just pigment alone.

skill.gen.paed.icterus.expect: Examine fully undressed in daylight. Note the lowest point of yellow, blanch the skin to see through dark complexions, and check the eyes and gums. Yellow to the thighs or soles in the first days is never trivial.

skill.exam.paed.weight.expect: Weigh undressed on the same scale and compare with birth weight. Excess loss marks poor intake, which both causes and worsens the yellow, and decides whether feeds alone can turn the course.

chapters.title: Neonatal examination
chapters.blurb: Zone the yellow, feel the belly, check the tone

skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.expect: Map the dermal zone head to toe and pair it with the bilirubin value and its trend. A zone that outruns the hours of age, or yellow with pale stools, moves the baby to testing and treatment without waiting.

skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.expect: Feel for a scalp swelling with defined margins and look for bruises anywhere. A cephalhaematoma is a slow-release load of pigment that deepens the yellow for days after an otherwise normal delivery.

skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.expect: Feel the liver edge and spleen tip: enlargement with pallor favours haemolysis, while a big liver with pale stools points toward blocked bile. Note a red or foul umbilical stump as the infective clue beside the yellow.

skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.expect: Separate true yellow from the red flush of a polycythaemic baby and the mottling of a cold one by blanching. Bruises, petechiae and pallor each name a different mechanism behind the colour.

stations.title: Assess the jaundiced newborn
stations.task: This 3-day-old term baby was brought with yellow colour noticed yesterday, now reaching the thighs. Examine the baby for jaundice and present your findings with the next step.
examinerQuestions: You mapped the yellow to the thighs on day three. What bilirubin range does that zone suggest, and why do you still need a blood test?
The stools are pale and chalky with dark staining urine. What does this change, and what single test settles it?
Name two behaviour findings that would make this an emergency rather than a routine referral.

stations.title: Take a jaundice history and counsel the mother
stations.task: This mother reports her 2-day-old baby looks yellow since this morning. Take a focused history in six minutes, state whether this is expected or disease, and counsel her on feeding and follow up.
examinerQuestions: Yellow appeared at 30 hours and is limited to the face in a vigorous feeder. Expected or disease, and what decides your answer?
The mother asks whether stopping breast milk will clear the yellow faster. How do you answer?
Which three risk answers would make you order a bilirubin test today rather than review tomorrow?

skill.reasoning.nj.basics.title: Why the newborn turns yellow
skill.reasoning.nj.basics.oneLine: Extra production, slow clearance, gut return: the three mechanisms
skill.reasoning.nj.basics.why: Jaundice is the commonest morbidity of the first week, touching most term and preterm babies, yet only a few carry disease. The student who holds the three mechanisms, extra production, slow clearance and gut return, can predict which yellow needs a test and which needs only a watch.

teach.heading: Three mechanisms, one yellow
teach.body: Newborn red cells break down faster and in greater numbers than adult cells, releasing pigment faster than the liver can handle. The newborn liver takes up pigment slowly and joins it to its carrier sluggishly, so unconjugated pigment builds in the blood. Slow stools return pigment from the gut to the blood instead of passing it out. Together they raise the level in 60 of 100 term and 80 of 100 preterm babies in the first week.

teach.heading: Why the brain is at stake
teach.body: Unconjugated pigment that is not carried on albumin can enter the brain, where it settles in the movement and hearing centres. Early effects show as sleepiness and poor feeding, then a shrill cry with shifting tone, arching of the back and neck, fits and laboured pauses in breathing. Survived injury leaves lasting movement disorder, hearing loss and upward gaze failure, which is why a rising level is treated before symptoms appear.

teach.heading: Expected versus disease, in one glance
points: Expected: face-only yellow on the second or third day, a vigorous frequent feeder, golden yellow stools, fading colour by two weeks.
Disease: yellow on the first day, fast deepening to the limbs and soles, a sleepy feeder, pale stools with dark urine, or colour still rising after two weeks.
The day of onset is the fastest separator: first-day yellow is always disease, while third-day face yellow in a well feeder is commonly expected.

pitfalls: Calling all early yellow expected because most newborn jaundice is, and missing first-day haemolysis.
Treating the colour as the disease instead of the pigment behind it, so the brain risk goes unmentioned.
Forgetting the gut return, so delayed stools and poor intake never enter the explanation.

probes.q: Name the three mechanisms that raise newborn bilirubin.
probes.a: Faster red cell breakdown with extra pigment production, slow liver uptake and conjugation, and return of pigment from the gut when stools pass slowly.

probes.q: Why is a rising bilirubin treated before the baby looks sick?
probes.a: Because free unconjugated pigment enters the brain and injures movement and hearing centres, and established injury is largely irreversible.

probes.q: How does day of onset alone separate expected from disease?
probes.a: First-day yellow is always disease, while face-only yellow on day two or three in a vigorous feeder is commonly the expected pattern.

skill.reasoning.nj.findings.title: Reading the yellow baby
skill.reasoning.nj.findings.oneLine: Zone estimates the level, stools name the type, behaviour stages the danger
skill.reasoning.nj.findings.why: The eye, the nappy and the cry together stage the illness: the zone estimates the level, the stool colour separates blocked bile from breakdown, and behaviour betrays brain involvement. The student who records all three never sends home a baby that needed light treatment.

teach.heading: Map the yellow head to toe
teach.body: Undress the baby fully and examine in daylight, blanching the skin with gentle finger pressure to see through dark complexions. Colour travels head to toe: face and neck first, then chest to the navel, then belly and thighs, then arms and legs below the knees, and finally palms and soles. The five zones track roughly 5, 10, 12 and 15 with more than 15 at the palms and soles, but the zone only triggers the blood test and never replaces it.

teach.heading: Stools, urine and the belly clue
teach.body: Golden yellow stools with clear urine fit unconjugated jaundice from breakdown or slow clearance. Pale chalky stools with dark staining urine mean conjugated pigment is reaching urine but not gut, which points to liver or bile duct blockage needing early referral. Feel the liver edge and spleen tip: enlargement with pallor favours haemolysis, and a big firm liver with pale stools favours blocked bile.

teach.heading: Behaviour is the emergency
points: A baby too sleepy to wake for feeds, with a weak suck, shows early brain effect and needs same-day testing.
A shrill cry with tone that swings between floppy and stiff, arching of the neck and back, marks advancing injury and needs emergency lowering of pigment.
Fits, pauses in breathing, or coma mean critical brain involvement with risk of lasting disability even after treatment.
Fever, fast breathing, or a red umbilical stump beside the yellow add infection to the picture and change the workup.

pitfalls: Grading yellow under yellow ward lights or through unblanched dark skin, and underreading deep jaundice.
Stopping at the face and missing palms, soles, stools and tone, which carry the staging.
Reassuring on colour alone while the baby is too sleepy to feed, which is brain involvement, not contentment.

probes.q: How do you map jaundice on the body, and what does each zone roughly mean?
probes.a: Blanch and read head to toe: face and neck, chest to navel, belly and thighs, limbs below knees, then palms and soles, tracking roughly 5, 10, 12, 15 and above 15.

probes.q: How do stools and urine separate blocked bile from ordinary newborn jaundice?
probes.a: Blocked bile gives pale chalky stools with dark staining urine, while ordinary unconjugated jaundice keeps golden yellow stools with clear urine.

probes.q: Which behaviour sequence marks advancing bilirubin injury to the brain?
probes.a: Sleepiness with poor feeding first, then a shrill cry with shifting tone and arching, then fits, breathing pauses or coma.

skill.reasoning.nj.summary.title: Summarising the yellow neonate
skill.reasoning.nj.summary.oneLine: Hours, zone, trend and cause in four sentences
skill.reasoning.nj.summary.why: A neonatal summary without hours of age and bilirubin trend leaves the listener unable to judge urgency. The four-sentence shape, baby with time, colour with trend, feeding with output, cause with plan, lets the consultant reach haemolytic disease before you name it.

teach.heading: The sentences in order
teach.body: State hours of age with gestation and weights first, since every threshold runs in hours. Add the colour with its zone and the bilirubin values with their direction across repeats. Give feeding and output in one line. Close with the cause statement, red flags present or absent, and the plan.

teach.heading: What must never be missing
points: Hours of age with gestation and birth weight, since thresholds differ for early and small babies.
Zone with bilirubin trend, not a single value, because a rising level behaves differently from a settled one.
Stool colour, urine colour and red flags, which separate blocked bile and brain involvement from ordinary yellow.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body: A 70-hour-old term boy, birth weight 2.9 kg, turned yellow at 30 hours with colour now to the thighs. Bilirubin has risen steeply across two tests. He feeds eight times a day but sleepily, with yellow stools and clear urine, and no fever or arching. Mother is group O and the baby group B with a positive antibody test. In summary: pathological unconjugated jaundice from ABO mismatch, for urgent light treatment with exchange readiness.

pitfalls: Giving age in days when every decision runs in hours, so urgency reads wrong.
Quoting one bilirubin value without trend, hiding a steep rise behind a moderate number.
Ending without the cause and the plan, leaving the summary a description rather than a decision.

probes.q: What four parts must a neonatal jaundice summary carry in order?
probes.a: Hours of age with gestation and weight, colour with zone and bilirubin trend, feeding with output, and the cause statement with red flags and plan.

rubric.text: States hours of age with gestation and weight
Gives zone with bilirubin trend, not a single value
Closes with the cause and the plan

skill.reasoning.nj.differential.title: Telling newborn yellow apart
skill.reasoning.nj.differential.oneLine: Nine lookalikes, each with the feature that rules it out
skill.reasoning.nj.differential.why: Most yellow in the first week is expected settling, but the dangerous minority hides inside the same colour: blood group disease, enzyme defects, infection and blocked bile each demand a different clock. The student who tests each mimic against one distinguishing feature treats none of them as ordinary yellow.

rows: ABO blood group mismatch
Group O mother with group A or B baby, positive antibody test, yellow within the first two days with anaemia
Rh haemolytic disease
Rh negative mother with Rh positive baby, often a previously affected sibling, early severe yellow with anaemia
G6PD enzyme deficiency
Family favism or drug-triggered anaemia, sudden deepening after an oxidant exposure or infection
Red cell membrane defects
Family history of lifelong mild jaundice with anaemia or early spleen removal, spherocytes on the film
Breastfeeding failure jaundice
Infrequent feeds with excess weight loss and few wet nappies in the first days, improving as intake improves
Breast milk jaundice
Well thriving baby with prolonged unconjugated yellow beyond two weeks and no other abnormality
Neonatal sepsis
Fever or low temperature, lethargy, poor perfusion or a red umbilical stump beside the yellow
Extravasated blood
Scalp swelling or bruising after instrumental delivery, yellow that deepens as the swelling resolves
Biliary atresia with cholestasis
Pale chalky stools with dark staining urine and a direct fraction above 2, needing early surgical referral
Congenital hypothyroidism
Prolonged yellow with sleepiness, poor activity, large tongue and delayed stooling, confirmed on thyroid testing

teach.heading: How to reason at the bedside
teach.body: Ask three questions in order. Did yellow appear on day one, which keeps only haemolysis and infection. Are stools pale with dark urine, which keeps only blocked bile. Is the baby thriving with prolonged yellow and nothing else, which keeps breast milk and thyroid causes. Whatever remains decides the first test, not the final label.

pitfalls: Calling prolonged yellow breast milk jaundice without checking stool colour and thyroid, missing blocked bile.
Missing sepsis because the yellow drew all attention and temperature and perfusion went unrecorded.
Treating poor intake yellow with water or formula top ups against advice instead of fixing breastfeeding.

probes.q: Which single history pair points to ABO mismatch?
probes.a: A group O mother with a group A or B baby, with yellow in the first two days and a positive antibody test.

probes.q: How do breastfeeding failure and breast milk jaundice differ in course?
probes.a: Failure shows in the first days with poor intake, weight loss and few nappies, while breast milk jaundice is prolonged yellow in a thriving baby beyond two weeks.

probes.q: Pale stools with dark urine in a 3-week-old. What is your next step?
probes.a: Test the direct bilirubin fraction at once and refer early for bile duct evaluation, since blocked bile is repaired against the clock.

rubric.text: Offers a differential spanning haemolytic, intake, infective and cholestatic causes
Uses stool and urine colour to separate blocked bile
Uses day of onset to narrow the field first

skill.investigation.nj.workup.title: Confirming and grading the yellow
skill.investigation.nj.workup.oneLine: Fractionate, group, plot against hours, repeat
skill.investigation.nj.workup.why: One bilirubin value without its fraction, its trend and the hours of age answers nothing: the fraction separates blocked bile from breakdown, the groups name haemolysis, and the hour chart grades urgency. Ordered in this sequence the tests answer one question each instead of confusing.

teach.heading: Total with fractions first
teach.body: Send total bilirubin with its direct fraction together: a direct fraction above 2 means conjugated disease and a different pathway, whatever the total. Where available, a skin reading screens but serum decides, since skin readings mislead in deep yellow and after light treatment has begun.

teach.heading: Name the breakdown
teach.body: Send mother and baby blood groups with the direct antibody test to catch mismatch disease. Add haemoglobin with reticulocytes and a blood film: falling haemoglobin with rising reticulocytes and spherocytes marks immune breakdown, while bite cells and blisters after illness or exposure mark enzyme deficiency. Test G6PD where family or course suggests it.

teach.heading: Plot against hours and look wider
teach.body: Plot every value against age in hours on the hour chart and repeat the test to fix the direction, since a steep rise behaves differently from a settled level. Early and small babies and unwell babies tolerate less, so their line sits lower. Add thyroid testing when yellow outstays two weeks, a sepsis screen with cultures when fever or lethargy travel with the yellow, and liver ultrasound when the fraction is conjugated.

pitfalls: Ordering total bilirubin alone, so conjugated disease hides inside a moderate total.
Testing once and acting on a single value, when the rise across repeats decides urgency.
Reading the value without hours of age, which is how a dangerous day-two level reads as safe.

probes.q: Why must every bilirubin request include the direct fraction?
probes.a: Because a direct fraction above 2 marks conjugated disease with liver or bile duct causes, needing a different pathway from ordinary unconjugated jaundice.

probes.q: Which blood results mark immune breakdown of red cells?
probes.a: Mother and baby group mismatch with a positive direct antibody test, falling haemoglobin with rising reticulocytes, and spherocytes on the film.

probes.q: When do you add thyroid and sepsis testing to the jaundice workup?
probes.a: Thyroid testing when yellow outstays two weeks with sleepiness and poor activity, and a sepsis screen with cultures when fever, lethargy or poor perfusion travel with the yellow.

skill.reasoning.nj.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and severity: the four rules and the hour chart
skill.reasoning.nj.diagnosis.oneLine: Four rules name disease, the hour chart grades it
skill.reasoning.nj.diagnosis.why: Calling yellow physiological without testing it against the four rules is how haemolysis, sepsis and blocked bile get sent home. The rules name disease in one line each, and the hour chart turns the bilirubin value into a treatment decision for this baby at these hours.

teach.heading: Four rules that name disease
points: Yellow within the first 24 hours of life is always pathological, most often blood group mismatch.
A rise of more than 5 in a day marks rapid breakdown needing urgent lowering, whatever a single value reads.
Yellow that persists beyond 14 days in a term baby needs a cause, with thyroid and conjugated disease on the list.
A direct fraction above 2 means conjugated disease of liver or bile duct, never ordinary newborn yellow.

teach.heading: Read the hour chart, not the number
teach.body: Plot the value against age in hours on the hour chart for the baby's gestation and risk: the same number behaves differently at 30 hours and at 5 days. A steep rise across repeats, or a level crossing the light treatment line, starts treatment without waiting for the next test. Early, small and unwell babies are treated at lower lines because their brains tolerate less.

teach.heading: Write the full statement
teach.body: Name the type, the cause where known, and the brain stage: pathological unconjugated jaundice from ABO mismatch with no encephalopathy, or prolonged conjugated jaundice with suspected bile duct blockage. Add the hour chart position and the trend, since the statement without them cannot drive the plan. A complete example: pathological unconjugated jaundice, ABO mismatch, above the light treatment line and rising, no encephalopathy signs.

pitfalls: Calling day-one yellow early physiological jaundice and reviewing tomorrow instead of testing today.
Acting on one value without the rise, so a steep climb hides behind a moderate number.
Stating the diagnosis without the cause and the hour chart position, leaving treatment undecided.

probes.q: Name the four rules that mark neonatal jaundice as pathological.
probes.a: Onset within 24 hours, a rise of more than 5 in a day, persistence beyond 14 days in a term baby, and a direct fraction above 2.

probes.q: Why must bilirubin be read against hours of age rather than alone?
probes.a: Because thresholds run in hours with gestation and risk, so the same value is dangerous at 30 hours and acceptable at 5 days.

probes.q: What does a complete diagnostic statement carry?
probes.a: The type with the cause where known, the brain stage, and the hour chart position with the trend.

rubric.text: Tests the yellow against all four pathological rules
Reads the value on the hour chart with trend
States type, cause, brain stage and position

skill.treatment.nj.care.title: Managing neonatal jaundice
skill.treatment.nj.care.oneLine: Feed, light, exchange readiness, and the cause beside the level
skill.treatment.nj.care.why: Light treatment started on the hour chart prevents brain injury, yet light alone fails the baby whose cause is sepsis, blocked bile or thyroid disease. The plan must lower the pigment and treat the cause together, with exchange ready before brain signs appear rather than after.
skill.treatment.nj.care.body: Support frequent breastfeeding first, start blue light phototherapy on the hour chart without delay, keep blood exchange ready for steep rises and brain signs, treat the underlying cause beside the level, and follow hearing and growth after discharge.

teach.heading: Feed, light and watch
teach.body: Feed eight to twelve times a day with waking for feeds, since good intake drives stooling that clears pigment. Nurse the undressed baby under blue lamps with covered eyes, keep feeds and fluids going, watch temperature and weight, and repeat bilirubin to track the fall. Recheck after stopping, since levels rebound and may need a second sitting.

teach.heading: Exchange, immunoglobulin and the cause
teach.body: A steep rise, a level near the exchange line, or any brain sign moves the baby to a newborn unit for double-volume blood exchange without delay. Isoimmune breakdown that keeps climbing despite light treatment is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin to slow red cell destruction. Sepsis gets antibiotics with cultures, prolonged jaundice gets thyroid testing and replacement where deficient, and conjugated disease gets early surgical referral.

teach.heading: Referral, family and follow up
teach.body:
Refer to the special newborn care unit when the hour chart line is crossed, the rise is steep, the fraction is conjugated, or brain signs appear. Sick newborn care in public facilities is free under the national newborn scheme.

Counsel the mother that breastfeeding continues through light treatment and that sunlight through windows is no substitute for lamps. After discharge, check hearing with brainstem testing and track growth and milestones, since early injury can declare itself late.

pitfalls: Delaying light treatment for repeat testing while the level climbs toward brain injury.
Stopping breast milk or giving water instead of increasing feed frequency under the lamps.
Treating the level while ignoring pale stools, fever or sleepiness, so blocked bile or sepsis runs untreated.

probes.q: What are the three arms of routine jaundice treatment?
probes.a: Frequent breastfeeding with waking for feeds, blue light phototherapy on the hour chart, and repeat bilirubin with a rebound check after stopping.

probes.q: When does a yellow baby need blood exchange rather than light alone?
probes.a: A steep rise, a level near the exchange line for age and risk, or any brain sign, managed in a newborn unit equipped for double-volume exchange.

probes.q: What follow up does a baby treated for severe jaundice need after discharge?
probes.a: Hearing testing with brainstem responses, growth and milestone tracking, and early surgical review where the fraction was conjugated.

skill.treatment.nj.care.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of modality and principle. Light treatment thresholds, lamp settings, exchange volumes and immunoglobulin dosing must be taken from your current institutional or national hour-chart guideline, such as the Indian Academy of Pediatrics guidance, and the treating paediatrician's prescription at the time of treatment. CliniX does not prescribe.

cases.title: Yellow since yesterday, now to the thighs
cases.opening: Sunita Pawar, 24, carries her 3-day-old son Aarav to the paediatric OPD of the taluka hospital. The baby looked yellow yesterday evening, and this morning the colour has reached his thighs. He feeds sleepily. Introduce yourself to the mother and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Aarav Pawar
patient.residence: Village near the taluka town, lives with parents and grandmother

what was the birth weight

delivery_events_bruise.reply: No instruments, labour was about six hours, no swelling on the head and no bruises. Nothing was needed after birth.

family_beans_drugs.reply: Nobody avoids any beans, no known anaemia in our families, and no operations of the spleen that I know.

maternal_health_meds.reply: No sugar problem, no thyroid problem. Only iron tablets in pregnancy. Labour started on its own, no injection for pains.

prior_tests_advice.reply: No blood test yet. The nurse at discharge said to show the baby if yellow reaches the legs. We kept him in morning sunlight today, which did not help.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.finding: Sleepy but rousable term newborn, lying quietly, pink peripherally with visible yellow of face and trunk. Cries weakly when unwrapped, settles quickly. No dysmorphism.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.finding: Temperature 37.4 C. Heart rate 148 per minute, regular. Respiratory rate 52 per minute. Blood pressure 68/42. SpO2 97 percent on room air. Brachial and femoral pulses felt equally.

skill.gen.paed.icterus.finding: Deep yellow of the face, eyes and gums in daylight, extending over the chest, belly and thighs to the knees. Palms and soles pink. No pallor of the tongue beyond the yellow.

skill.exam.paed.weight.finding: Weight 2.7 kg undressed on the infant scale, against a birth weight of 2.9 kg. Length and head circumference appropriate for gestation.

skill.exam.paed.neo.jaundice_kramer.finding: Dermal zone 3 on blanching: colour to the lower abdomen and thighs, sparing palms and soles. Sclerae and oral mucosa yellow. Stools golden yellow, urine dark yellow staining the nappy.

skill.exam.paed.neo.head_skull_trauma.finding: No scalp swelling, no cephalhaematoma, no bruising. Anterior fontanelle flat and open. Sutures normally opposed.

skill.exam.paed.neo.abdomen_genitalia_sp.finding: Liver edge 1 cm below the costal margin, soft. Spleen tip not felt. No abdominal distension. Umbilical stump dry with no redness. Spine straight with no dimple or swelling.

skill.exam.paed.neo.skin_cord_variations.finding: No bruises, petechiae or rashes. Cord stump clean and dry. No pallor of creases beyond the yellow tinge.

skill.gen.paed.pallor.finding: Mild pallor of the tongue and conjunctivae seen through the yellow tinge.

skill.exam.paed.neo.primitive_reflexes.finding: Moro response present but weak, rooting and sucking present with a weak suck. Tone normal, no arching, no opisthotonus. No fits observed.

tsb_total.label: Total serum bilirubin with repeat
tsb_total.result: 18.4 at 70 hours, up from 12.1 at 48 hours. Plotted above the light treatment line for a term well baby and still rising.
tsb_total.note: The trend across two tests decides here, not one value: a steep rise to zone 3 colour needs light treatment without waiting.

direct_fraction.label: Direct bilirubin fraction
direct_fraction.result: 0.6 with total 18.4. Unconjugated pattern, no cholestasis.
direct_fraction.note: A low direct fraction keeps this in the unconjugated pathway; a fraction above 2 would have meant liver or bile duct disease instead.

bloodgroup_dat.label: Mother and baby blood groups with direct antibody test
bloodgroup_dat.result: Mother O positive, baby B positive, direct antibody test positive.
bloodgroup_dat.note: This names the mechanism: ABO mismatch with ongoing immune breakdown, matching the sibling pattern and the early onset.

haemoglobin_retic.label: Haemoglobin with reticulocyte count
haemoglobin_retic.result: Haemoglobin 14.5 with reticulocytes 6 percent and spherocytes on the film.
haemoglobin_retic.note: Falling haemoglobin with a reticulocyte response and spherocytes confirms haemolysis rather than slow clearance alone.

smear_film.label: Peripheral blood film
smear_film.result: Spherocytes with polychromasia, no blister or bite cells, no blasts.
smear_film.note: Spherocytes fit immune breakdown; bite cells would have pointed to enzyme deficiency instead.

g6pd_screen.label: G6PD screening
g6pd_screen.note: Sent because any haemolytic course deserves it, and a normal result keeps the blame on the ABO mismatch.

thyroid_test.label: Thyroid function
thyroid_test.note: Not indicated on day three with an explained haemolytic cause; thyroid testing belongs to yellow that outstays two weeks.

sepsis_screen.label: Sepsis screen with blood culture
sepsis_screen.result: C reactive protein normal, counts unremarkable, culture sent and pending. Baby afebrile with normal perfusion.
sepsis_screen.note: Reasonable in any pathological course to avoid missing infection, though nothing here points to sepsis as the driver.

differentialModel.answer: Pathological unconjugated neonatal jaundice from ABO mismatch. Consider Rh haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, neonatal sepsis, breast milk jaundice if prolonged, biliary atresia excluded by yellow stools and low direct fraction, and congenital hypothyroidism if yellow persists.
accept: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn
Rh haemolytic disease of the newborn

diagnosis.answer: Pathological unconjugated neonatal jaundice from ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn, above the light treatment line and rising, with early neurobehavioural changes and no advanced encephalopathy.
accept: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn

managementModel.answer: Support frequent breastfeeding with waking for feeds, start blue light phototherapy at once under lamps with eye cover and repeat bilirubin, keep blood exchange ready for a steep rise or brain signs, arrange newborn unit review with hearing follow up, and counsel the mother that feeds continue through treatment.

teachingPoints: The clock makes the diagnosis before any test: yellow at 30 hours with a group O mother and group B baby is haemolysis until proven otherwise.
Zone 3 colour with a steep rise across two tests needs light treatment at once; the trend, not one value, drives the decision.
Mild pallor with spherocytes and a positive antibody test confirms breakdown, while golden stools with a low direct fraction exclude blocked bile without further tests.
Sleepiness with a weak suck is early brain effect, not contentment, which is why this baby is treated urgently rather than reviewed tomorrow.
A sibling who needed light treatment is the history that predicts the course; ask it in every newborn with yellow.
Sunlight through windows does not substitute for lamps, and breastfeeding continues through treatment with waking for feeds.
